title: How Music Works

learn.summary: All music is organized sound: pitch (how high), rhythm (when), and timbre (what it sounds like). Western music tunes A above middle C to 440 Hz and splits every octave into 12 equal semitones. Understanding these three ingredients lets you decode any song you hear.

do: Pick one song you love and write down three things you hear: the pulse, the melody instrument, and one background layer.

children.title: Sound & Pitch

learn.summary: Pitch is vibration frequency measured in hertz: concert A is 440 Hz, and doubling any frequency (440 to 880 Hz) produces the same note an octave higher. That octave equivalence is why note names repeat A through G. Low bass notes sit around 40–100 Hz; a soprano's high C is about 1047 Hz.

do: Install a free tuner app, hum a steady note, and watch the hertz readout — then hum it an octave higher and confirm the number roughly doubles.

children.title: Why 12 Notes

learn.summary: Equal temperament divides the octave into 12 semitones, each multiplying frequency by the 12th root of 2 (about 1.0595). It is a deliberate compromise: pure ratios like 3:2 are slightly bent so that every key sounds equally in tune. This 18th-century trade-off is why a piano can play in all 24 keys without retuning.

do: On a piano app, play all 12 semitones from C up to B in order, then say each note name aloud — sharps and all.

children.title: Active Listening

learn.summary: Musicians listen in layers, not in a wash. A typical pop track has four: drums, bass, chords (guitar or keys), and melody (voice). Training yourself to isolate one layer at a time is the single fastest ear upgrade available, and it costs nothing.

do: Play one song three times today: first time follow only the drums, second only the bassline, third only the melody.
